intro: Long ago, in many parts of the world, the family you were born into set your place in life. A king's child grew up to rule. A farmer's child grew up to farm. In this unit you will visit castles in England, samurai in Japan, scholars in China, and rulers of the Aztec and Inca.

Then you will come to today. You will learn words like income, wealth and opportunity. You will see why some people and countries have more than others. You will also meet the neighbors, libraries and food banks that help.

By the end, you will be able to explain how ranks by birth worked and how they changed. You will be able to name reasons people have more or less. And you will be able to share your own idea about what makes a chance fair, using facts.
bigQuestion: How did being rich or poor work long ago, how does it work now, and what makes a fair chance?

timeline.t: Confucius teaches in China about family, learning and good behavior
English nobles make King John agree to Magna Carta
English peasants march to London in the Peasants' Revolt
The Aztec and Inca empires are at their largest
Japan's rulers set samurai apart as the top rank
China ends its old civil service exams
The United Nations says everyone has the right to education
World Bank: about 1 in 10 people live in extreme poverty

words.d: a person's place in a group, from high to low
a way of sorting people into ranks, like steps on a ladder
a king or queen who rules a country
a member of a powerful family with land and a title
a peasant tied to a lord's land who could not leave without permission
a warrior in Japan who served a lord and was born into that rank
money that comes in over time, like pay from a job
everything a person owns, minus what they owe
something you own that has value, like a home or a business
a group that helps people and does not try to make a profit
money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services
a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a job

test.why: China used civil service exams to choose officials.

test.q: How were Japan's merchants and samurai different from about 1600 to the 1860s?
choices: Samurai ranked higher, but some merchants were richer
test.why: Samurai ranked at the top, but some low-ranked merchants became very rich.

test.q: What was mit'a in the Inca Empire?

test.why: Mit'a was the Inca duty of taking turns working for the state.

test.q: Why did the Black Death give peasants more power?
choices: It left fewer workers, so their work was needed more
test.why: With far fewer workers, lords needed the peasants who survived.

choices: Even the king must follow the law
test.why: Magna Carta said even the king had to follow the law.

test.q: What is the difference between income and wealth?
choices: Wealth is only pay from a job
Income is money coming in; wealth is all you own minus what you owe
Income is a house; wealth is a paycheck
test.why: Income comes in over time; wealth is what you own minus what you owe.

Less schooling always means higher pay

write.prompt: Is it fairer today than long ago for a child to choose their own path in life? Make a claim. Use two or three facts from the unit, like serfdom, the Peasants' Revolt, public libraries or the World Bank numbers, to explain it.
tips: Start with one clear sentence that says your claim.
Name where each fact comes from, like the World Bank or Magna Carta.
Give one reason someone might see it differently.
Use unit words like rank, opportunity and wealth.

title: Rich and Poor, Then and Now

chapters.title: Kings, Nobles and Peasants Long Ago
chapters.bigQuestion: What was life like when the family you were born into decided your place?

story.title: Agnes Carries the Water
story.kicker: It is a cold morning in England in the year 1300. Agnes has a job to do.
paragraphs: The sun is just coming up. Agnes is ten years old. She lives in a small village in England. The year is 1300. Her house has one room and a roof made of straw. Her family shares it with a pig and some hens.
Agnes picks up two wooden buckets. She walks down the muddy path to the stream. She fills the buckets. They are heavy. Water splashes on her feet. She starts the long walk home.

On the hill stands the lord's castle. It has thick stone walls and a tall tower. Flags wave from the top. Agnes has never been inside. The lord owns the land her family farms. Her father works his fields three days each week.

A rider in fine clothes trots past. It is the lord's son. He does not look at Agnes. She steps off the path and waits. One day he will own the castle. One day Agnes will carry water for her own children.
Agnes thinks about this as she walks. Who decided that he lives in a castle? Who decided that she carries water? No one asked either of them. They were both born into their places.
story.think: Agnes and the lord's son were born into different lives. What do you think each of them would want to change?

lessons.title: What Is a Rank?
lessons.mainIdea: Long ago, in many places, the family you were born into set your rank in life.
reading: Think about Agnes and the lord's son. They lived in the same village. But their lives were very different. He rode a horse and lived in a castle. She carried water and lived in a hut. The difference came from their families.

A *rank* is a person's place in a group, from high to low. When people are sorted into ranks like steps on a ladder, we call it a *hierarchy*. The top step had the most power and wealth. The bottom step had the least.

In many places long ago, you stayed on the step where you were born. A farmer's child usually became a farmer. A noble's child became a noble. This was true in Europe, Asia, Africa and the Americas. It began to change only slowly.

words.d: a person's place in a group, from high to low
a way of sorting people into ranks, like steps on a ladder

look.title: A Ladder of People
look.text: Picture a tall ladder. At the top stands a king with a crown. A few steps down stand nobles in fine cloaks. Below them stand knights with swords. At the bottom, the widest step, stand many farmers holding hoes. There are far more people at the bottom than at the top.
look.prompt: Why do you think the bottom step of this ladder holds the most people?

check.q: What is a hierarchy?
choices: A way of sorting people into ranks from high to low
A kind of castle with a tall tower
A job that a farmer does in spring
A law that makes everyone equal
check.why: A hierarchy sorts people into ranks, like steps on a ladder.

check.q: Long ago, what usually decided a person's rank?
choices: A test they took at school
The family they were born into
The town they chose to move to
check.why: The reading says the family you were born into set your rank.

check.q: In the story, why did Agnes carry water while the lord's son rode a horse?
choices: The lord's son was older and stronger
They were born into different ranks
Agnes lost a race to him
check.why: Their lives were different because they were born into different families and ranks.

lessons.title: Kings and Queens
lessons.mainIdea: A king or queen ruled a kingdom, and the crown usually passed to their child.
reading: In 1272, a man named Edward became King of England. He did not win an election. His father had been king before him. When Edward died, his son became king next. That is how the crown moved in many kingdoms.

A *monarch* is a king or queen who rules a country. A monarch often ruled for life. When the crown passes down to a child, we say the rule is *inherited*. You get it from your family, the way you might get your grandmother's ring.

Monarchs made laws, led armies and collected taxes. Many said God had given them the right to rule. But a monarch could not rule alone. They needed nobles, soldiers and farmers. That need gave other people some power too.

words.d: a king or queen who rules a country
passed down to you from your family

look.title: Two Ways to Get a Leader
look.text: Kingdom A: The old king dies. His oldest child is crowned the next day. Nobody votes. Town B: The old mayor finishes her time in office. The people line up and vote. The person with the most votes becomes the new mayor.
look.prompt: How is choosing a leader in Kingdom A different from Town B?

check.q: What is a monarch?
choices: A farmer who works the lord's field
A king or queen who rules a country
A soldier who guards a castle
A person who votes in an election
check.why: A monarch is a king or queen who rules.

check.q: How did Edward become King of England in 1272?
choices: He inherited the crown from his father
check.why: The reading says his father had been king before him, so the crown passed down to him.

check.q: Why could a monarch NOT rule alone?
choices: They needed nobles, soldiers and farmers
They were not allowed to make laws
They lived only a short time
They had no money at all
check.why: The reading says monarchs needed nobles, soldiers and farmers, which gave those people some power.

lessons.title: Nobles and Knights
lessons.mainIdea: Nobles got land from the king and promised loyalty and soldiers in return.
reading: A king could not watch over every field and village. So he gave big pieces of land to powerful families. In return, each family promised to be loyal. They also promised to send soldiers when the king went to war.

These powerful families were *nobles*. They had titles like lord, lady, duke or earl. Many nobles trained *knights*. A knight was a soldier who fought on horseback in armor. Knights promised to serve their lord.

Nobles often lived in castles. A castle was a strong home made of stone. It had thick walls to keep enemies out. It showed everyone nearby who was in charge. Life inside was not always comfy. Castles were cold and smoky.

words.d: a member of a powerful family with land and a title, like lord or duke
a soldier who fought on horseback in armor and served a lord

look.title: A Promise Chain
look.text: The king gives land to a lord. The lord promises: I will be loyal and send you soldiers. The lord gives a smaller piece of land to a knight. The knight promises: I will fight for you. Farmers work all the land and give food to the lord.
look.prompt: Follow the chain. Who gives land, and who gives service back?

check.q: What did nobles promise the king in return for land?
choices: To pay for a new castle for the king
To grow all the king's food themselves
To be loyal and send soldiers
check.why: Nobles promised loyalty and soldiers when the king went to war.

check.q: What is a knight?
choices: A soldier who fought on horseback in armor
A farmer who owns a mill
A stone tower on a castle
check.why: A knight was a soldier on horseback in armor who served a lord.

check.q: What did a castle show the people who lived nearby?
check.why: The reading says a castle showed everyone nearby who was in charge.

lessons.title: Peasants and Serfs
lessons.mainIdea: Most people were peasants who farmed, and many serfs could not leave the land they worked.
reading: Agnes's family were *peasants*. Peasants were farmers who worked the land. In Europe long ago, most people were peasants. They grew wheat, oats and beans. They kept pigs, sheep and hens.

Many peasants were *serfs*. A serf was tied to a lord's land. A serf could not move away without the lord saying yes. Serfs worked the lord's fields for part of each week. They also gave the lord part of their own crops.

The lord's land and village together were called a *manor*. A manor had fields, a mill, a church and houses. Serfs were not slaves. In most places, they could not be sold one by one. They had their own homes and families. But they were not free to choose their life.

words.d: a farmer who worked the land, often for a lord
a peasant who was tied to a lord's land and could not leave without permission
a lord's land, with its fields, mill, church and village

look.title: A Week for a Serf
look.text: Monday, Tuesday and Wednesday: plow the lord's field. Thursday: fix the fence around the family's own strip of land. Friday and Saturday: plant beans in the family's strip. Sunday: go to church. At harvest time, carry some of the family's grain to the lord.
look.prompt: How much of this serf's week went to the lord? What might that feel like?

check.q: What made a serf different from other peasants?
choices: A serf lived in a castle
A serf could not leave the lord's land without permission
A serf did not farm at all
A serf was a kind of knight
check.why: Serfs were tied to the lord's land and needed permission to leave.

check.q: What was a manor?
choices: A crown worn by a queen
A lord's land with its fields, mill, church and village
A kind of tax paid in coins
check.why: The reading says a manor was the lord's land and village together.

check.q: How were serfs different from slaves?
choices: Serfs could not be sold one by one and had their own homes
Serfs did no work for anyone
Serfs were free to move anywhere
check.why: The reading says serfs could not be sold one by one and had their own homes and families.

lessons.title: Emperor, Shogun and Samurai
lessons.mainIdea: In Japan, samurai warriors served powerful lords, and people were sorted into ranks by birth.
reading: Japan had an emperor. People honored him. But for hundreds of years, a military ruler called the *shogun* held the real power. Under the shogun were great lords. Each lord had warriors who served him.
These warriors were the *samurai*. Samurai trained with swords and bows. They were taught to be loyal, brave and calm. Many also studied poetry and writing. Being a samurai passed from father to son.

From about 1600 to the 1860s, Japan's rulers kept samurai apart as the top rank. Official teaching listed farmers next, then craft workers, then merchants who bought and sold. Merchants were ranked low, yet some became very rich. Wealth and rank did not always match.

words.d: a military ruler who held the real power in Japan for hundreds of years
a warrior in Japan who served a lord and was born into that rank

look.title: Rich but Ranked Low
look.text: Picture a merchant in the city of Osaka in the 1700s. He sells rice and cloth. His storehouse is full. He lends money to a samurai family who needs it. Still, by law, the samurai ranks above him. The samurai may wear two swords. The merchant may not.
look.prompt: In this scene, who has more money? Who has higher rank? Why might that seem strange?

check.q: Who held the real power in Japan for hundreds of years?
check.why: The reading says the shogun, a military ruler, held the real power.

check.q: Which group was at the top of Japan's ranks from about 1600 to the 1860s?
check.why: Samurai were ranked at the top.

check.q: What surprising fact does the reading share about merchants in Japan?
choices: They were ranked low, yet some became very rich
They were ranked highest of all
They were the same as samurai
check.why: Merchants were ranked low, but some became very rich, so wealth and rank did not always match.

lessons.title: Emperor and Scholars in China
lessons.mainIdea: In China, scholars who passed hard tests could become officials who helped the emperor rule.
reading: China had an emperor who ruled a huge land. He needed many helpers to run it. For over a thousand years, China chose many helpers in a special way. It gave hard written tests.

The tests were called the *civil service exams*. Students spent years reading old books, like the teachings of Confucius. Confucius was a teacher who lived about 2,500 years ago. He taught respect for family, learning and good behavior.

People who passed became *scholar-officials*. They helped run towns and provinces. Scholars had high rank and respect. In theory, many boys could take the tests. In practice, rich families could pay for more years of study. Girls were not allowed to take them.

words.d: hard written tests China used to choose government officials
a learned person who passed the exams and helped run the government

look.title: Confucius on Learning
look.text: Is it not a joy to learn something and then practice it again and again?
look.cite: Confucius, The Analects, Book 1 (sayings collected by his students, compiled after his death)
look.prompt: Why would a teacher who said this be important to students studying for a test?

check.q: How did China choose many of its officials?
choices: By drawing names from a hat
By who owned the most horses
check.why: China used the civil service exams, hard written tests, to choose officials.

check.q: Who was Confucius?
choices: A teacher who taught respect for family and learning
check.why: The reading says Confucius was a teacher who taught respect for family, learning and good behavior.

check.q: Why did rich families have an advantage with the exams?
choices: They could pay for more years of study
They got the answers ahead of time
The tests were only given in castles
check.why: The reading says rich families could pay for more years of study.

lessons.title: Aztec Rulers and Commoners
lessons.mainIdea: The Aztec had a ruler, nobles and commoners, and most people farmed or worked with their hands.
reading: About 500 years ago, a great city stood on an island in a lake. It was Tenochtitlan, the home of the Aztec. Today Mexico City stands in the same place. Canals ran through it like streets.

The Aztec ruler was called the *tlatoani*, which means speaker. He led the army and the temples. Below him were nobles. Nobles could wear cotton clothes and gold jewelry. Most people were *commoners*. They farmed, fished, built and made crafts.
Commoners belonged to neighborhood groups. Each group shared land and ran a school for its boys. A brave commoner could rise by doing well in war. That gave some people a way to move up.

words.d: the Aztec ruler; the word means speaker
an ordinary person who is not a noble or ruler

look.title: Two Aztec Neighbors
look.text: Picture two people in Tenochtitlan. One wears a soft cotton cloak and a gold lip ornament. He sits near the ruler. The other wears a rough cloak made of plant fiber. She carries corn to the market in a canoe.
look.prompt: Which person is a noble and which is a commoner? What clues tell you?

check.q: What does tlatoani mean?
check.why: The reading says tlatoani means speaker.

check.q: Where did Tenochtitlan stand?
choices: On an island in a lake, where Mexico City is now
Next to a castle in England
check.why: Tenochtitlan was on an island in a lake, where Mexico City stands today.

check.q: How could an Aztec commoner move up?
check.why: The reading says a brave commoner could rise by doing well in war.

lessons.title: The Inca and Shared Work
lessons.mainIdea: The Inca ruler was at the top, and families paid their share by working for the state.
reading: High in the Andes Mountains of South America, the Inca built a large empire. About 500 years ago, it ran along the mountains for thousands of miles. Its ruler was the *Sapa Inca*. People treated him as holy.
The Inca did not use coins. Instead, families paid by working. This duty was called *mit'a*. Men took turns building roads, bridges and walls. Some served as soldiers. Some worked in mines.

In return, the state kept food in big storehouses. It could feed people in a bad year. Nobles and officials watched over the work. Most families farmed their own land too. Rank came mostly from birth, as in Europe and Japan.

words.d: the ruler of the Inca Empire
the Inca duty of taking turns working for the state instead of paying money

look.title: Paying With Work
look.text: A farmer in the Andes gets word. It is his family's turn. He leaves his potato field for some weeks. He helps build a stone road across the mountains. His neighbors will take the next turn. Later that year, frost kills many crops. The state storehouse sends food to his village.
look.prompt: What did the farmer give? What did his village get back?

check.q: What was mit'a?
choices: A duty to take turns working for the state
check.why: Mit'a was the duty of taking turns working for the state instead of paying money.

check.q: Who was the Sapa Inca?
choices: The ruler of the Inca Empire
check.why: The Sapa Inca was the ruler of the Inca Empire.

check.q: How did the Inca state help people in a bad year?
choices: It fed them from big storehouses
check.why: The reading says the state kept food in storehouses and could feed people in a bad year.

lessons.title: Peasants Push Back
lessons.mainIdea: After a terrible plague, workers were scarce, and English peasants demanded more freedom.
reading: In 1348, a terrible sickness reached England. People called it the *Black Death*. It was a plague, a disease that spread fast. Fleas helped spread it. Across Europe, it killed about one third of the people, or maybe more.

After the plague, there were far fewer workers. Lords needed help in their fields. Some peasants asked for higher pay. Some moved to find better work. Lords and the king tried to stop them with new laws.

In 1381, thousands of English peasants marched to London. This was the *Peasants' Revolt*. They wanted an end to serfdom. The young king met them and made promises. Then he broke them. Still, over the next hundred years, serfdom in England slowly faded away.

words.d: a deadly plague that swept across Europe starting in the 1340s
a 1381 uprising in England where peasants marched to demand freedom

look.title: A Preacher's Question
look.text: When Adam dug the earth and Eve spun thread, who was the nobleman then?
look.cite: Words linked to John Ball, a priest who spoke to the rebels in the Peasants' Revolt, 1381
look.prompt: Adam and Eve are the first people in the Bible story. What point is the speaker making about nobles?

check.q: Why did peasants gain some power after the Black Death?
choices: There were far fewer workers, so lords needed them
check.why: The plague killed so many people that workers were scarce, and lords needed help.

check.q: What did the peasants want in the 1381 revolt?
check.why: The reading says they wanted an end to serfdom.

check.q: What happened to serfdom in England over the next hundred years?
choices: It ended the very next day
check.why: The reading says serfdom in England slowly faded away over the next hundred years.

lessons.title: Old Ranks Begin to Fade
lessons.mainIdea: Over hundreds of years, many countries ended ranks set by birth and gave more people rights.
reading: In 1215, English nobles made King John agree to a paper called *Magna Carta*. It said even the king had to follow the law. At first it helped mostly nobles. Later, people used its ideas to claim rights for everyone.

Change came in many places, often very slowly. Russia freed its serfs in 1861. Japan ended the samurai as a ruling rank in the 1870s. China stopped its old exams in 1905. Each change had its own story and its own struggles.

Today, most countries say people are *equal* under the law. Birth still affects people's lives in many ways. But a farmer's child can become a doctor, a teacher or a leader. People worked and argued for a long time to make that possible.

words.d: a 1215 English agreement that said even the king must follow the law
having the same rights and value as others

look.title: From Magna Carta
look.text: No free man shall be arrested, jailed or have his land taken, except by the lawful judgment of his equals or by the law of the land.
look.prompt: Who does this promise protect? Why might people later want it to cover everyone?

check.q: What did Magna Carta say about the king?
choices: He could do anything he wanted
He had to follow the law too
He must live in a manor
check.why: Magna Carta said even the king had to follow the law.

check.q: Which country freed its serfs in 1861?
check.why: The reading says Russia freed its serfs in 1861.

check.q: What does equal under the law mean?
choices: Everyone lives in the same house
Everyone has the same rights under the law
check.why: Equal means having the same rights and value; under the law, the same rules apply to all.

review.q: In medieval Europe, what was a serf?
choices: A king's helper who ran a province
A peasant tied to a lord's land
review.why: A serf was a peasant who could not leave the lord's land without permission.
Samurai were warriors in Japan. The other pairs mix up places and terms.

review.q: How was China's way of choosing officials different from Europe's nobles?
choices: China used a vote by farmers
China chose the best sword fighters
review.why: China used civil service exams, while European nobles mostly got power by birth.

review.q: What did the Inca use instead of coins to collect what the state needed?
review.why: Inca families paid by taking turns working, a duty called mit'a.

review.q: What gave English peasants more power after 1348?
choices: The Black Death left fewer workers
They won a war against France
The king made them all nobles
review.why: The plague killed so many that workers were scarce, so their work was worth more.

review.q: In Japan from about 1600 to the 1860s, which group was ranked low even though some got rich?
review.why: Merchants were ranked low, yet some became very rich.

review.q: What is one thing Magna Carta, the end of serfdom in Russia, and the end of China's old exams have in common?
choices: They all happened in the same year
They were all changes to old systems of rank and power
They all made one family rule forever
review.why: Each was a step in changing old systems of rank and power.

choices: A promise between a lord and a knight
A way of sorting people into ranks from high to low
A city built on a lake
review.why: A hierarchy sorts people into ranks, like steps on a ladder.

chapters.title: Why Some People Have More
chapters.bigQuestion: Why do some people and places have more than others, and what makes a chance fair?

story.title: Two Cousins, One Dream
story.kicker: Luis and Marisol are cousins. Both want to be doctors. They live in two different countries.
paragraphs: Luis is eleven. He lives in Chicago. Every morning he rides a yellow bus to school. His school has a science lab and a nurse's office. Luis loves the nurse's office. He wants to be a doctor one day.

His cousin Marisol is also eleven. She lives in a small mountain town in Honduras, in Central America. She walks almost an hour to school. Her class shares a few old books. Marisol wants to be a doctor too.

Both cousins are smart. Both work hard. Both help at home. On Sundays they talk on a video call. Luis shows her a model of a heart from his library. Marisol tells him about the clinic in the next town. It is open only two days a week.
Marisol's family grows coffee. In a good year, they sell a lot. In a year with too little rain, they sell less. Then her parents worry about money for her school shoes and bus rides to high school.
The two cousins have the same dream. They have the same grandparents. Yet the road ahead looks different for each of them. Why is that? This chapter looks for answers.
story.think: Luis and Marisol have the same dream. What things might make that dream easier or harder for each of them?

lessons.title: Income and Wealth
lessons.mainIdea: Income is money you get over time; wealth is everything you own, minus what you owe.
reading: Ms. Park is a bus driver. Every two weeks she gets a paycheck. That paycheck is her *income*. Income is money that comes in over time. It can come from a job, a business or other places.

Ms. Park also owns things. She has a small house, a car and some money in the bank. All that she owns, minus what she owes, is her *wealth*. If she still owes money on her house, that part is not really hers yet.

Income and wealth are not the same. A person can earn a good income but own little. Another person can own a farm but have a small income this year. Both words help us understand who has more, and why.

words.d: money that comes in over time, like pay from a job
everything a person owns, minus what they owe

look.title: Sort It Out
look.text: Look at this list: a weekly paycheck, a house, money earned selling lemonade this summer, a bicycle, a savings account, a tip from a customer.
look.prompt: Which items are income coming in? Which are part of someone's wealth?

check.q: What is income?
choices: Money a person owes the bank
Money that comes in over time, like pay
check.why: Income is money that comes in over time, like a paycheck.

check.q: Ms. Park owns a house and a car and has money in the bank. What word describes all of this, minus what she owes?
check.why: Wealth is everything a person owns, minus what they owe.

check.q: Which statement from the reading is true?
choices: Income and wealth always go together
A person can have a good income but own little
Wealth is only money in a pocket
check.why: The reading says a person can earn a good income but own little.

lessons.title: Saving and Owning
lessons.mainIdea: Saving money and owning things like land or a business can help wealth grow over time.
reading: Mr. Okafor opened a small bakery. First he saved part of his pay for five years. Then he used the savings to rent a shop and buy an oven. Now the bakery earns money every day.

*Saving* means keeping some money instead of spending it now. Savings can be used later to buy things that earn money. A shop, a farm or a building can earn money for years. Things you own that have value are called *assets*.

Wealth often grows when people own assets. A family that owns a home can pass it to its children. That gives the children a head start. A family with no assets starts from zero. This is one reason wealth gaps can last a long time.

words.d: keeping some money to use later instead of spending it now
something you own that has value, like a home, land or a business

look.title: Two Paths for $100
look.text: Ana gets $100 for her birthday. Path 1: she spends it all on a game this week. Path 2: she saves it. Next summer she uses it to buy a used lawn mower. She mows neighbors' lawns and earns $20 each time.
look.prompt: Which path could help Ana earn more money later? Why?

check.q: What is an asset?
choices: Something you own that has value
check.why: An asset is something you own that has value, like a home or a business.

check.q: How did Mr. Okafor start his bakery?
choices: He saved part of his pay for years
He found an oven on the street
check.why: He saved part of his pay for five years, then used the savings to start.

check.q: Why can wealth gaps between families last a long time?
choices: Assets like homes can be passed to children
Banks give money only on Mondays
check.why: Families with assets can pass them down, giving their children a head start.

lessons.title: Training and Pay
lessons.mainIdea: Jobs that need more training or school often pay more, on average.
reading: Dr. Reyes is a nurse practitioner. She studied for about seven years after high school. Her friend works at a store. He started right after high school. On average, Dr. Reyes earns more.

Jobs that need special skills often pay more. The skills take years of *training* or school to learn. Also, fewer people can do those jobs. When something is needed and hard to find, people often pay more for it.

This is an average, not a rule. Some people with little schooling start businesses and earn a lot. Some people with lots of schooling earn little. And many jobs that pay less, like caring for children, are very important. Pay is not the same as value.

words.d: learning the skills needed for a job
a typical amount found by adding numbers and dividing by how many there are

look.title: School and Weekly Pay in the U.S.
look.cite: U.S. Bureau of Labor Statistics, Education Pays, 2023 data
look.prompt: About how much more per week does a typical worker with a four-year degree earn than one with a high school diploma?

check.q: Why do jobs that need special skills often pay more?
choices: The skills take years to learn, and fewer people can do them
The government picks their pay by lottery
check.why: The reading says the skills take years to learn and fewer people can do those jobs.

check.q: In the chart, which group earns the most per week?
check.why: The Master's degree row shows the highest number, about $1,740.

check.q: What does the reading mean by 'Pay is not the same as value'?
choices: Some important jobs, like caring for children, pay less
check.why: The reading says many jobs that pay less, like child care, are very important.

lessons.title: Luck and Where You Are Born
lessons.mainIdea: Luck and the place and family you are born into also shape how much people have.
reading: Remember Luis and Marisol. They are both smart and hard-working. But Luis goes to a school with a lab. Marisol walks an hour to a school with few books. Neither cousin chose where to be born.

*Luck* is what happens to you by chance, not by choice. Being born in a rich country is luck. So is a storm that ruins a farm, or a sickness in the family. Good luck and bad luck can both change a family's money.
Hard work and choices matter a lot. So does luck. Most experts agree that both play a part. People disagree about how much each one counts. That question is part of many debates about fairness.

words.d: things that happen to you by chance, not by your choice
the way things can happen without anyone planning them

look.title: A Storm on the Farm
look.text: Two farmers live side by side. Both plant corn. Both work from sunrise to sunset. In July, a hailstorm crosses the fields. It flattens one farmer's corn. It misses the other farmer's field by a few feet.
look.prompt: Did one farmer work harder than the other? What made the difference?

check.q: What is luck?
choices: Things that happen by chance, not by choice
check.why: Luck is what happens to you by chance, not by your choice.

check.q: In the hailstorm example, why did one farmer lose the corn?
choices: The storm hit his field by chance
check.why: Both worked equally hard; the storm hit one field by chance.

check.q: What does the reading say about hard work and luck?
choices: Both play a part, and people disagree about how much each counts
check.why: The reading says both play a part and people disagree about how much each counts.

lessons.title: Being Poor Is Not Who You Are
lessons.mainIdea: Being poor means having too little money for needs; it is not a sign of a person's worth.
reading: Jada's mom lost her job when her company closed. For a few months, money was very tight. Jada still did her homework. Her mom still made dinner. They were the same kind, hard-working people as before.

Being *poor* means not having enough money for basic needs. *Needs* are things people must have to live, like food, a safe home, clothes and health care. Many families are poor for a while, then things get better.

Being poor does not tell you who a person is. It does not mean they are lazy or less smart. Many causes, like a closed factory, an illness or low pay, can lead to it. Every person deserves respect, whatever their money.

words.d: not having enough money for basic needs
things people must have to live, like food, a safe home, clothes and health care

look.title: What Would You Say?
look.text: At lunch, a student says, 'Kids who get free lunch must have lazy parents.' Another student knows her dad works two jobs. Her family still qualifies for free lunch.
look.prompt: Using the reading, what could someone say to answer the first student kindly and truthfully?

check.q: Which of these is a basic need?
choices: A trip to an amusement park
check.why: Needs are things people must have to live, like a safe home.

check.q: Why did Jada's family have less money for a few months?
choices: They spent it all on toys
check.why: The reading says her mom lost her job when her company closed.

check.q: According to the reading, what does being poor tell you about a person?
choices: That they will always be poor
It does not tell you who they are
check.why: The reading says being poor does not tell you who a person is.

lessons.title: Food Banks and Neighbors
lessons.mainIdea: Food banks and other groups collect food and share it with people who need it.
reading: On Saturday morning, Tom and his dad sort cans at a food pantry. They put beans in one box and soup in another. Later, families come in and choose what they need.

A *food bank* is a big warehouse that collects food. It gets food from farms, stores and people who give. It sends the food to smaller *food pantries* in neighborhoods. Chicago has a large one, the Greater Chicago Food Depository.

Many food banks are run by *charities*, groups that help people and do not try to make a profit. Churches, mosques, temples and neighbors help too. Volunteers give their time. Anyone might need help someday, and anyone can help.

words.d: a big warehouse that collects food and sends it to places that share it
a neighborhood place where families can pick up food they need
a group that helps people and does not try to make a profit

look.title: Follow the Can of Soup
look.text: A farmer grows tomatoes. A company makes them into soup. A grocery store has extra cans. It gives them to the food bank. A truck takes them to a pantry at a church. A grandmother picks up a can for dinner.
look.prompt: Name each stop the soup made. Where could a volunteer help along the way?

check.q: What does a food bank do?
choices: Collects food and sends it to pantries
Sells food for a big profit
check.why: A food bank collects food and sends it to smaller pantries.

check.q: What is a charity?
choices: A group that helps people and does not try to make a profit
check.why: A charity helps people and does not try to make a profit.

check.q: What large food bank does the reading name in Chicago?
check.why: The reading names the Greater Chicago Food Depository.

lessons.title: Schools and Libraries for All
lessons.mainIdea: Public schools and libraries give everyone a chance to learn, no matter how much money they have.
reading: After school, Mei goes to her neighborhood library. She borrows books and uses a computer for homework. It costs her nothing. Her library card is free.

A *public library* is open to everyone and paid for by taxes. *Taxes* are money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services. The Chicago Public Library opened in 1873. Today it has branches all over the city.

Public schools are paid for by taxes too. In the United States, every child can go to school for free. Many people believe free schools and libraries help make chances fairer. A child with no books at home can still read every day.

words.d: a library open to everyone and paid for by taxes
money people and businesses pay to the government for shared services

look.title: A Promise to Every Person
look.text: Everyone has the right to education.
look.cite: United Nations, Universal Declaration of Human Rights, Article 26, 1948
look.prompt: How do public schools and libraries help keep this promise?

check.q: How are public libraries paid for?
choices: By a fee each time you borrow
check.why: Public libraries are paid for by taxes.

check.q: When did the Chicago Public Library open?
check.why: The reading says the Chicago Public Library opened in 1873.

check.q: Why do many people believe free schools and libraries make chances fairer?
choices: A child with no books at home can still read every day
check.why: The reading says a child with no books at home can still read every day.

lessons.title: Rich and Poor Countries
lessons.mainIdea: Countries differ a lot in wealth, and the share of people in extreme poverty has fallen over time.
reading: In some countries, most homes have running water and electricity. In others, many families carry water from a well. Marisol's town in Honduras has a clinic open two days a week. Luis's city has many hospitals.

Some people live in *extreme poverty*. The World Bank uses that term for living on only a couple of dollars a day. In 1990, more than one in three people in the world lived this way. By 2019, it was about one in ten.

Why did this happen? Many countries grew more food, built factories and sent more children to school. Trade between countries grew too. People still debate which causes mattered most. Hundreds of millions of people still live in extreme poverty.

words.d: living on so little money that it is hard to meet basic needs; the World Bank sets a dollar line for it
buying and selling goods between people or countries

look.title: Share of the World in Extreme Poverty
look.cite: World Bank, Poverty and Inequality Platform estimates ($2.15-a-day line, 2017 prices)
look.prompt: What happened to the share of people in extreme poverty from 1990 to 2019?

check.q: About what share of the world lived in extreme poverty in 1990?
check.why: The reading and chart show about 38 percent, which is more than one in three.

check.q: Which group measured the numbers in the chart?
check.why: The chart cites the World Bank.

check.q: What does the reading say about the causes of the drop in extreme poverty?
choices: There were many causes, and people debate which mattered most
check.why: The reading lists several causes and says people still debate which mattered most.

lessons.title: What Is Fair?
lessons.mainIdea: Opportunity means having a real chance, and people have different ideas about what makes chances fair.
reading: Picture a race. One runner starts at the line. Another starts ten steps behind. Both run hard. Is the race fair? Most people would say no. The runners did not have the same start.

*Opportunity* is a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a good job. *Fairness* means treating people in a way that is right and just. Many people say a fair country gives every child a real opportunity.

People agree on a lot, but not everything. Some say fair means the same rules for everyone. Some say fair means extra help for those who start behind. Many people believe some of both. Good thinkers listen to each side.

words.d: a real chance to do something, like go to school or get a job
treating people in a way that is right and just

look.title: Two Ideas of Fair
look.text: Idea 1: Give every student the same book and the same test. Same rules for all is fair. Idea 2: Give every student the same test, but give a student who needs glasses a pair first. Helping each person reach the start line is fair.
look.prompt: What is good about each idea? When might you use each one?

check.q: What is opportunity?
choices: A real chance to do something
check.why: Opportunity is a real chance to do something, like go to school.

check.q: Why does the race in the reading seem unfair?
choices: One runner starts ten steps behind
check.why: The runners did not have the same start.

check.q: What does the reading say good thinkers do about different ideas of fairness?
check.why: The reading says good thinkers listen to each side.

lessons.title: Different Ideas About Helping
lessons.mainIdea: People disagree about who should help most: families, charities, businesses or the government.
reading: A town has a problem. Some families cannot afford food. The town meets to talk. One neighbor says the church and food pantry should help. Another says the government should run a program. A store owner offers to hire more workers.

People have different ideas about who should help. Some think *government* programs, paid for by taxes, work best for big problems. They say help should reach everyone. Others think families, charities and businesses help best. They say local people know their neighbors' needs.

Each view has supporters and critics. Most countries use a mix. In the United States, food pantries, churches, businesses and government programs all help. Adults debate the right mix at every election.

words.d: the group of people and offices that make and carry out laws for a place
a planned service, like one that helps families buy food

look.title: The Town Meeting
look.text: Speaker 1: 'Our taxes should pay for a food program. Then no family is missed.' Speaker 2: 'Our churches and pantries know each family. They can help faster and with a personal touch.' Speaker 3: 'More jobs in town would help families earn their own money.'
look.prompt: What is one strong point each speaker makes? Could the town use more than one idea?

check.q: What do some people say is good about government programs?
choices: They are run by one family
check.why: Supporters say government programs can reach everyone.

check.q: What do some people say is good about help from charities and neighbors?
choices: They are run by a king
Local people know their neighbors' needs
check.why: Supporters say local people know their neighbors' needs.

check.q: What do most countries do, according to the reading?
choices: Use a mix of ways to help
check.why: The reading says most countries use a mix.

review.q: Which is an example of income?
review.why: Income is money that comes in over time, like a paycheck. The others are things owned.

review.q: What is the difference between a food bank and a food pantry?
choices: A food bank collects food; a pantry shares it with families nearby
A pantry is a warehouse; a bank is a store

choices: One does not want to be a doctor

review.q: Which of these is an asset?
review.why: An asset is something you own that has value, like a business.

review.q: What does the chart from the Bureau of Labor Statistics show?

It means you are less smart

review.q: Two people disagree. One says the same rules for all is fair. The other says extra help for those who start behind is fair. What is this debate about?
